Derivatives of the optimal solution with respect to parameters

Source: R/solution-derivatives.R
opt_solution_jacobian.Rd

Differentiates the optimal point \(x^*(p)\) and optimal value \(f^*(p)\) of a continuous model with respect to parameters, by the implicit function theorem applied to the KKT conditions on the active set at the solution. With \(H\) the Hessian of the Lagrangian \(L = f - y^\top g\) in the free variables (those not at a bound), \(J_A\) the Jacobian of the active rows and \(y_A\) their multipliers, the derivatives solve $$\begin{pmatrix} H & -J_A^\top \\ J_A & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} dx/dp \\ dy_A/dp \end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix} \nabla^2_{xp} L \\ \partial g_A / \partial p \end{pmatrix}$$ and \(df^*/dp = \partial L / \partial p\) (envelope theorem). All second derivatives are exact.

Usage

opt_solution_jacobian(result, parameter, tol = 1e-07)

Arguments

result

A solved opt_result with a primal solution.

parameter

A parameter expression or name.

tol

Tolerance for active rows, bounds and zero multipliers.

Value

A list with solution (matrix: variables by parameter elements), objective (gradient of the optimal value), active (names of active rows and bounds) and multipliers ("solver" or "estimated").

Details

The result is valid when the solution is a strict local optimum that satisfies linear independence of the active constraint gradients (LICQ), the second-order sufficient condition and strict complementarity. The function stops when the KKT matrix is singular (LICQ or second-order sufficiency fails) and warns when an active row or bound has a zero multiplier (strict complementarity fails, so the solution map may only have one-sided derivatives). The active set is held fixed, so the derivatives are local: a large parameter change can change the active set. Mixed-integer and conic models are refused; for a mixed-integer model, differentiate the opt_fixed_relaxation() instead.

Examples

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
p <- opt_parameter(m, "p", value = 1)
opt_constraint(m, sum(x) <= p, name = "budget")
opt_objective(m, sum((x - c(2, 1))^2))
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_solution_jacobian(r, p)  # dx/dp = (0.5, 0.5)
#> $solution
#>        p
#> x[1] 0.5
#> x[2] 0.5
#> 
#> $objective
#>  p 
#> -2 
#> 
#> $active
#> [1] "budget"
#> 
#> $multipliers
#> [1] "solver"
#>
